questions.question: What does it mean for a polynomial to factor over F_p?
options: It splits into lower-degree polynomials with coefficients in F_p
It evaluates to zero at every possible coefficient in F_p
It has leading coefficient one after modular reduction
It uses powers larger than the chosen field characteristic
questions.explanation: Factoring over F_p means writing the polynomial as a product of lower-degree polynomials whose coefficients are also in F_p.

questions.question: Why is irreducibility needed when constructing F_p[x]/(m) as a field?
options: It prevents nonzero elements from becoming zero divisors
It makes every coefficient list have the same length
It changes polynomial addition into integer addition
It removes the need for modular coefficient arithmetic
questions.explanation: If m factors, the quotient can contain nonzero zero divisors. Irreducibility is what makes the quotient a field.

questions.question: What does finding a root r of f(x) over F_p immediately tell you?
options: A root r shows that x-r divides the polynomial
A root r proves every coefficient must be zero
A root r makes the polynomial automatically monic
A root r changes the coefficient field size
questions.explanation: The factor theorem says that f(r)=0 means x-r divides f(x). This gives a direct reducibility witness.

questions.question: Why are root checks not enough for every irreducibility test?
options: A quartic can split into two quadratic factors
A quartic cannot be evaluated over finite fields
A quartic always has four visible linear roots
A quartic has no meaningful leading coefficient
questions.explanation: For degree at least four, a polynomial may factor without having a linear factor. A root check only detects linear factors.

questions.question: What is the core move in Rabin's irreducibility criterion?
options: Check Frobenius powers and gcds modulo f
Try random integer division until one works
Count coefficient lists shorter than f only
Compare decimal encodings of the polynomial
questions.explanation: Rabin's criterion checks Frobenius powers of x modulo f and uses gcds to rule out lower-degree factors.

questions.question: What should happen to x^(p^n) modulo an irreducible degree-n polynomial f?
options: x^(p^n) reduces back to x modulo f
x^(p^n) becomes the constant zero
x^(p^n) lists all roots in order
x^(p^n) removes the leading term
questions.explanation: In the degree-n extension field, every element satisfies a^(p^n)=a. Testing this on x is part of the irreducibility check.

questions.question: What is the concrete attack witness when a reducible modulus is accepted?
options: Find nonzero factors whose product is zero
Choose a larger prime for faster exponentiation
Pad each coefficient list with extra zeros
Replace every inverse with ordinary division
questions.explanation: If m=a*b, then a and b are nonzero in the quotient but multiply to zero. That breaks field-style division assumptions.

questions.question: Why should ExtensionField reject a reducible modulus before arithmetic starts?
options: Later division may silently face noninvertible values
Addition would stop reducing coefficients modulo p
The polynomial degree would become hard to print
Root searches would always return empty lists
questions.explanation: Reducible moduli create zero divisors, so some nonzero values lack inverses. Rejecting the modulus prevents fake-field arithmetic.
